w: Profit primarily flows into owners' equity through retained earnings when not distributed; whether it affects liabilities at all depends on subsequent decisions (e.g., declaring a dividend creates a liability, using profit to repay debt reduces liabilities) — so profit does not have one fixed automatic effect on liabilities.

s:
Mr. Raj owns a sole proprietorship. During the year he:
• Paid his personal life insurance premium through the business bank account.
• Purchased office furniture from his personal savings.
• Withdrew ₹15 lakh for construction of his residence.
• Paid business loan instalments through the business account.
The accountant argues that all these transactions represent business expenses because the proprietor and business are legally the same. Which accounting concept contradicts this view?
o: Historical Cost Concept
Going Concern Concept
Business Entity Concept
Money Measurement Concept
w: Recording only the business's own transactions separately from the owner's personal transactions — treating the business as a distinct unit from its proprietor — is an application of the Business Entity Concept, one of the fundamental accounting concepts.

s: GreenPower Equipments Ltd. installed pollution-control machinery costing ₹12 crore. The State Government sanctioned a capital subsidy of ₹3 crore to promote environmentally sustainable manufacturing. The subsidy was received after the machinery had already been installed and commissioned. The Accounts Executive proposes crediting the entire subsidy to the Statement of Profit and Loss because "cash has been received during the current year." The CFO disagrees. Which accounting treatment is most appropriate under AS 12?
o: Credit the subsidy directly to Share Capital because it strengthens the financial position.
Recognise the subsidy immediately as Other Income because every Government grant is revenue in nature.
Treat the subsidy as a grant related to a depreciable asset by either deducting it from the carrying amount of the asset or recognising it as deferred income, as permitted under AS 12.
Keep the subsidy outside the financial statements until the useful life of the machinery expires.
w: Under AS 12, a grant related to a depreciable fixed asset should be accounted for either by reducing the grant from the asset's cost (so future depreciation is charged on the net amount) or by treating it as deferred income and recognising it in the Statement of Profit and Loss over the asset's useful life — it should not be taken to income immediately or credited to Share Capital.

s:
Metro Infra Ltd. entered into a fixed-price contract for construction of a flyover. At the end of Year 1:
• Contract Price : ₹220 crore
• Estimated Total Cost : ₹180 crore
• Cost Incurred till Date : ₹72 crore
• Physical Completion : 40%
• Outcome of the contract can be estimated reliably.
The Project Accountant recommends recognising revenue only after completion because no final bill has yet been raised. The Statutory Auditor disagrees. Which accounting principle best supports the auditor's view?
o: Revenue should be recognised only when cash is received.
Revenue should always be postponed until the customer formally accepts the completed project.
Construction contracts are governed exclusively by AS 9.
Revenue from construction contracts should generally be recognised based on the stage of completion where the outcome can be estimated reliably.
w: AS 7 requires revenue and costs on construction contracts to be recognised by reference to the stage of completion (percentage-of-completion method) as work progresses, provided the outcome of the contract can be estimated reliably, rather than waiting until final acceptance or cash receipt.

s:
Alpha Biotech Ltd. incurred the following expenditure while developing a new pharmaceutical product:
• Basic scientific research.
• Development after technical feasibility was established.
• Patent registration fees.
• Advertising before commercial launch.
The Finance Manager proposes capitalising all expenditure because every item contributes to future profitability. Which statement best reflects AS 26?
o: Every expenditure relating to the same project should be capitalised.
Research expenditure is generally expensed, whereas qualifying development expenditure may be recognised as an intangible asset after satisfying recognition criteria.
Advertising expenditure always creates an intangible asset.
Patent registration expenditure should always be written off immediately.
w: Under AS 26, all research expenditure must be expensed as incurred since future economic benefits cannot be demonstrated at that stage, whereas development expenditure may be recognised as an intangible asset only if it satisfies specific recognition criteria (technical feasibility, intention and ability to complete and use/sell the asset, etc.).

s: Horizon Traders discounted a 90-day Bills Receivable with its banker before maturity. The trainee accountant passed the following entry: Bank A/c Dr. Discount A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c The Senior Accountant reviewed the entry. Which observation is correct?
o: Only the bank should record the transaction.
The entry is incorrect because Sales Account should also be credited.
Bills Receivable should never be credited before maturity.
The entry correctly records replacement of Bills Receivable with cash while recognising discount as a finance cost.
w: When a Bill Receivable is discounted with the bank before maturity, the entry correctly replaces the Bills Receivable asset with cash received, while the difference (discount) is recognised as a finance/discounting charge in the Statement of Profit and Loss, since the underlying sale had already been recorded earlier.

s:
On 31 March 2026, the Cash Book shows a favourable bank balance. The following items are identified:
• Outstanding cheque issued.
• Bank charges debited by the bank.
• Direct deposit by a customer.
• Dishonoured cheque not yet recorded in the Cash Book.
Which items require adjustment in the Cash Book before preparing the BRS?
o: Outstanding cheque only.
Bank charges only.
Bank charges, direct deposit and dishonoured cheque.
Outstanding cheque and dishonoured cheque.
w: Items such as bank charges debited directly by the bank, amounts directly deposited by a customer into the account, and cheques that were recorded as collected but later dishonoured, are all entries that appear in the bank's books but not yet in the depositor's Cash Book, requiring adjustment in the Bank Reconciliation Statement — as opposed to a simple outstanding (unpresented) cheque, which is a mere timing difference alone.

s:
Skyline Developers is constructing a commercial complex expected to take four years. At the end of Year 2:
• Work completed : 52%
• Future costs can be estimated reliably.
• Customer has certified 50% of the work.
The Project Manager insists that profit should not be recognised until the building is fully completed. Which Accounting Standard primarily governs recognition in such cases?
o: AS 7 -- Construction Contracts
AS 3 -- Cash Flow Statements
AS 10 -- Property, Plant & Equipment
AS 9 -- Revenue Recognition
w: AS 7 specifically deals with the recognition of revenue and costs associated with long-duration construction contracts, prescribing the percentage- of-completion method as the primary basis for recognition — distinct from AS 9 (general revenue recognition) or AS 3 (cash flows).

s:
purchased a kiln. Subsequent expenditure included:
• Freight
• Installation
• Routine maintenance
• Replacement of a major component increasing useful life
The Accounts Executive proposes capitalising all expenditure. Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Capitalise every expenditure incurred during the first year.
Capitalise nothing after the asset is commissioned.
Capitalise freight, installation and replacement of the major component; charge routine maintenance to revenue.
Capitalise only freight and installation.
w: Under AS 10, expenditure that enhances the asset's future economic benefits — such as freight and installation on acquisition, or replacement of a major component that improves or extends the asset's working life — is capitalised, while routine maintenance that merely keeps the asset working as originally intended is charged to revenue.

s:
A machine was purchased for ₹48 lakh.
Additional Information:
• Installation : ₹2 lakh
• Residual Value : ₹5 lakh
• Useful Life : 9 years
The company proposes selling the machine after three years. Ignoring taxation, what is the carrying amount immediately before sale?
o: ₹40 lakh
₹35 lakh
₹36.50 lakh
₹38.50 lakh
w: Depreciable amount = cost incl. installation − residual = (48 + 2) − 5 = ₹45 lakh. Annual SLM = 45/9 = ₹5 lakh. After 3 years: 50 − 15 = ₹35 lakh.

s: Atlas Engineering Ltd. revises the estimated useful life of a machine after obtaining a technical report indicating faster technological obsolescence. The Finance Executive proposes recalculating depreciation from the date of acquisition and restating previous financial statements. Which accounting treatment is correct?
o: Restate previous financial statements.
Depreciation method cannot be revised.
Adjust the difference directly against retained earnings.
Apply the revised estimate prospectively because it represents a change in accounting estimate.
w: A revision in an asset's useful life is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy or a correction of an error; under AS 5, such changes are applied prospectively — spreading the remaining depreciable amount over the revised remaining useful life — without restating prior years' financial statements.

s:
On 31 March 2026, Nova Enterprises reported the following:
• Cash Book Balance : ₹24.80 lakh
Additional Information:
• Outstanding cheques : ₹4.20 lakh
• Dishonoured cheque not yet recorded : ₹1.10 lakh
• Bank charges debited : ₹12,500
• Dividend directly credited by bank : ₹95,000
• Insurance premium paid by bank under standing instruction : ₹48,000
The trainee accountant proposes including all five items only in the Bank Reconciliation Statement without passing any adjustment entries. Which statement is technically correct?
o: No adjustment is required until the bank issues revised statements.
Dishonoured cheque, bank charges, direct dividend credit and standing instruction require Cash Book adjustments, while outstanding cheques remain timing differences.
All five items are timing differences.
Only bank charges require adjustment.
w: A dishonoured cheque, bank charges debited by the bank, a dividend directly credited by the bank, and payments made under a standing instruction are all transactions that the bank has recorded but the depositor has not yet entered in the Cash Book, so they require correcting entries in the Cash Book itself — unlike an outstanding (unpresented) cheque, which is a simple timing difference that will clear itself and needs no Cash Book correction.

s:
During audit, the following transactions were identified:
1. Purchase of office furniture debited to Purchases Account.
2. Annual maintenance expenditure capitalised.
3. Legal expenses for acquiring land debited to Land Account.
4. Freight incurred for bringing machinery to the factory debited to Freight Outward Account.
Which of the above represent Errors of Principle?
o: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
All four
2 and 3 only
w: An Error of Principle occurs when a transaction is recorded by violating a fundamental accounting principle (such as treating a capital item as revenue, or vice versa) even though the double entry itself balances; applying that definition to the transactions in the scenario, Transactions 1, 2 and 4 are identified as principle errors, while Transaction 3 is not.

s:
Vertex Manufacturing Ltd. entered into the following transactions:
1. Purchased machinery through bank.
2. Paid installation wages.
3. Purchased lubricants for routine servicing.
4. Received insurance claim for damage to machinery.
5. Exchanged an old machine for a new one.
The Accounts Executive debited Machinery Account in every transaction involving machinery. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Whenever bank is involved, the Golden Rules become irrelevant.
Installation wages should always be charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Only expenditure creating or enhancing future economic benefits should be capitalised; routine servicing should be charged to revenue.
Every payment relating to machinery should be capitalised.
w: Applying the Golden Rules, only expenditure that creates a new asset or genuinely enhances/extends the future economic benefit of an existing asset (like machinery) should be capitalised; routine servicing and maintenance costs that merely keep the asset in its normal working condition are revenue expenditure and must be charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

s:
ABC India Pvt. Ltd. purchases specialised components from its overseas parent company. The Transfer Pricing Officer observes:
• Purchase prices are substantially above comparable uncontrolled prices.
• Indian taxable profits are significantly reduced.
• Pricing follows internal group policy.
Which principle forms the basis of Transfer Pricing adjustment?
o: Group companies are free to determine any transfer price.
Customs valuation automatically determines Income-tax valuation.
Transactions between associated enterprises should ordinarily satisfy the Arm's Length Principle.
Transfer Pricing provisions apply only to domestic transactions.
w: Under transfer pricing regulations, transactions between associated (related) enterprises must generally be priced as if they were between unrelated parties, i.e., they must satisfy the Arm's Length Principle, to prevent profit shifting through artificially set prices between group entities.

s:
following independent transactions occurred:
1. Purchased office furniture on credit.
2. Paid outstanding electricity charges through bank.
3. Received cash from a debtor after allowing discount.
4. Purchased machinery by issuing equity shares.
A trainee proposes:
• Debit Purchases Account in Transaction 1.
• Debit Outstanding Electricity Account in Transaction 2.
• Debit Discount Allowed Account in Transaction 3.
• Debit Machinery Account in Transaction
4.
Which evaluation is technically correct?
o: Transaction 1 is incorrect because furniture is a capital asset, whereas Transactions 2, 3 and 4 are correctly analysed.
All four journal treatments are incorrect.
Only Transactions 2, 3 and 4 are correctly analysed.
Transactions 1 and 2 are correct.
w: Furniture is a capital (fixed) asset, so purchasing furniture should be debited to a Furniture (asset) account, not treated as a revenue/expense item as done in Transaction 1 — making that entry incorrect — while Transactions 2, 3 and 4 apply the standard debit/credit rules correctly.

s: A machine costing ₹3,00,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum under the Written Down Value Method. The company proposes selling the machine after three complete years. Ignoring taxation, the Written Down Value immediately before sale is closest to:
w: Under the Written Down Value Method, depreciation is charged each year at a fixed percentage on the asset's reducing book value (not on original cost); applying the applicable rate over the relevant years as per the figures given results in a closing book value of ₹1,53,600.

s:
A Chartered Accountant identifies the following Accounting Standards:
• Government Grants
• Cash Flow Statements
• Intangible Assets
• Property, Plant and Equipment
The Managing Director asks: Which Accounting Standard primarily governs recognition and measurement of tangible fixed assets, and which governs classification of cash flows?
o: AS 26 and AS 12
AS 10 and AS 3
AS 3 and AS 26
AS 12 and AS 26
w: AS 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) governs the recognition, measurement and capitalisation of fixed assets, while AS 3 (Cash Flow Statements) governs the classification and presentation of cash flows — together these are the two standards that best match the business situations typically presented in such integrated scenarios.

s:
A transport company purchases 500 electric buses. The technical report concludes:
• Highest utilisation during initial years.
• Maintenance expenditure increases in later years.
• Economic benefits are consumed more rapidly in early years.
Which depreciation method best reflects this pattern?
o: Inventory Method
Straight Line Method
Revaluation Method
Written Down Value Method
w: The Written Down Value Method charges a higher depreciation amount in the earlier years of an asset's life (when its economic benefit/usage is typically higher, as with transport vehicles that see heavier wear early on) and progressively lower amounts later, aligning the depreciation charge more closely with the actual pattern of the asset's consumption of economic benefits.

Two identical machines costing ₹25 lakh each are purchased on the same date.
• Machine A –- Straight Line Method
• Machine B –- Written Down Value Method \@20% At the end of the third year, the CFO compares their carrying amounts.
Which statement is generally correct?
o: Machine B is likely to have the lower carrying amount because WDV recognises higher depreciation during earlier years.
Comparison is impossible because different methods are used.
Machine A will necessarily have the lower carrying amount.
Both machines must have identical carrying amounts.
w: WDV at 20%: 25 × 0.8³ = ₹12.8 lakh after 3 years. SLM gives a lower book value only if life is short (e.g. life under about 6 years). For normal lives WDV writes off more in early years, so Machine B is likely to have the lower carrying amount.

s:
Omega Manufacturing Ltd. purchased an automated robotic arm for ₹2.40 crore. The company estimated:
• Useful Life: 8 years
• Residual Value: Nil
The Finance Controller remarks: "At the end of the useful life, the carrying amount of the asset should become zero." The Cost Accountant disagrees and argues that this outcome depends upon the depreciation method adopted. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Under the Straight Line Method with nil residual value, the carrying amount can reduce to zero at the end of the useful life.
Residual value has no relevance in determining depreciation.
Depreciation methods cannot reduce the carrying amount below the original residual value.
Under the Written Down Value Method, every depreciable asset necessarily reaches zero carrying amount.
w: Under the Straight Line Method, if the residual (salvage) value is taken as nil, equal depreciation is charged each year over the useful life so that the asset's carrying amount is fully written down to zero by the end of that period — unlike the Written Down Value Method, which mathematically never reduces the carrying amount to exactly zero.

s: Vertex Engineering Ltd. drew a bill of exchange on 10 January 2026, payable 90 days after date. The Accounts Officer records the maturity date as exactly 90 days after the bill date. The Internal Auditor objects. Ignoring public holidays, which statement is correct?
o: Three days of grace are generally added while determining the maturity date of a time bill.
Days of grace apply only to demand bills.
Time bills mature exactly after the specified period.
Days of grace are applicable only when specifically mentioned in the bill.
w: Traditionally, three additional days (known as 'days of grace') are added beyond the tenure specified in a time bill of exchange while computing its legal due/maturity date, a convention recognised under the Negotiable Instruments Act, unlike demand bills which are payable on presentation.

s:
A company entered into the following transactions:
• Sale to a wholly owned subsidiary.
• Purchase from an unrelated listed company.
• Interest-free loan to the Managing Director.
• Rent paid to a partnership firm in which a director is a partner.
The Finance Manager proposes disclosing only the transaction with the subsidiary. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Transactions with related parties covered under AS 18 require disclosure in accordance with the Standard.
Related Party Disclosure is necessary only when profit arises.
Only cash transactions require disclosure.
Only subsidiary transactions require disclosure.
w: AS 18 requires an enterprise to disclose material transactions it has entered into with related parties (not just subsidiaries, and irrespective of whether the transactions were in cash or resulted in profit), so that users of financial statements can assess the impact such relationships may have had on the reporting entity.

s:
A consulting firm follows the Cash Basis of accounting. During March:
• Consultancy fees earned remain outstanding.
• Office rent for next month is paid in advance.
• Electricity expense relating to March remains unpaid.
The auditor recommends adopting the Accrual Basis. Which explanation is most appropriate?
o: Cash Basis cannot recognise fixed assets.
Cash Basis is prohibited for every business entity.
Accrual accounting recognises income and expenses in the period to which they relate, resulting in a more faithful measurement of profit.
Accrual accounting records only credit transactions.
w: Accrual accounting recognises income when earned and expenses when incurred, matching them to the period to which they actually relate regardless of when cash is received or paid, which gives a more faithful and complete picture of an entity's true financial performance than the Cash Basis, which recognises transactions only when cash moves.

s:
While preparing the Bank Reconciliation Statement, the accountant discovers:
• A cheque deposited was recorded in the Cash Book as ₹18,000 instead of ₹1,80,000.
• Bank charges debited by the bank have not been recorded.
• A cheque issued remains unpresented.
• Interest credited by the bank has not been entered in the Cash Book.
The junior accountant proposes treating all four items merely as reconciling items. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Only the posting error requires correction.
Posting error, bank charges and bank interest require correction in the Cash Book, whereas the unpresented cheque represents a timing difference.
All four items should remain only in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.
Bank Reconciliation Statement cannot be prepared until every error is corrected.
w: A posting error, bank charges debited by the bank, and interest charged/credited by the bank are all items where the depositor's Cash Book needs to be corrected to reflect the true position, whereas an unpresented (outstanding) cheque is simply a timing difference that will resolve itself once presented and needs no Cash Book correction, only disclosure in the Bank Reconciliation Statement.

s:
The Trial Balance of Vertex Industries Ltd. showed a difference of ₹3,42,000, which was temporarily transferred to a Suspense Account. During investigation, the following errors were identified:
1. Cash received from a debtor ₹1,25,000 was correctly entered in the Cash Book but posted to the debtor's account as ₹1,52,000.
2. Sales Book total was undercast by ₹48,000.
3. Purchase Return of ₹36,000 was correctly entered in the journal but omitted from the supplier's account.
4. Salary paid ₹84,000 was posted twice to Salary Account.
The Finance Executive comments: "Every correction involving the Suspense Account ultimately affects the company's profit." Which statement is technically correct?
o: Incorrect, because Suspense Account merely facilitates temporary balancing of one-sided errors; many corrections affect only ledger balances and not profit.
Correct, because every posting error changes the Statement of Profit and Loss.
Correct, because Suspense Account is opened only for revenue-related errors.
Incorrect, because Suspense Account is used only while preparing Bank Reconciliation Statements.
w: The Suspense Account is merely a temporary balancing tool used to make a Trial Balance agree when one-sided errors are discovered; many rectification entries involving the Suspense Account affect only ledger account balances (like correcting a wrongly posted amount) and do not necessarily alter the reported profit figure at all.

ABC Ltd. has issued ₹60 crore, 9% Debentures, redeemable after 6 years. The Board creates a Sinking Fund by investing fixed annual amounts in Government Securities.
The CFO makes the following observations:
1. A Sinking Fund spreads the financial burden of redemption over several years.
2. Income earned on Sinking Fund investments increases the amount available for redemption.
3. Creation of a Sinking Fund removes the legal obligation to redeem debentures on maturity.
4.
The primary objective is to ensure availability of funds for redemption. Which combination is correct?
o: All four statements
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
w: A sinking fund sets aside fixed amounts each year and invests them, so the redemption burden is spread (1) and investment income adds to the fund (2); its purpose is to have cash ready at redemption (4). It does not remove the legal obligation to redeem (3 wrong).

s:
Delta Engineering Ltd. purchased machinery costing ₹1.80 crore. Original estimates:
• Useful Life : 10 years
• Residual Value : ₹20 lakh After five years, a revised technical report estimates the residual value at ₹8 lakh, while the remaining useful life remains unchanged. The Accounts Officer proposes recalculating depreciation for all previous years. The Statutory Auditor disagrees. Which accounting treatment is correct?
o: The revision represents a change in accounting estimate and should be applied prospectively over the remaining useful life.
The reduction should be adjusted directly against General Reserve.
Residual value becomes irrelevant after the asset is put to use.
Previous years' depreciation should always be recomputed whenever residual value changes.
w: A change in the estimated salvage (residual) value of an asset is treated as a change in accounting estimate under AS 5, and is applied prospectively — the remaining depreciable amount (cost less revised residual value less accumulated depreciation) is spread over the asset's remaining useful life, without restating depreciation already charged in prior years.

s:
The Trial Balance of Omega Components Ltd. agreed on 31 March 2026. Audit reveals the following independent errors:
• Machinery purchased for ₹9,80,000 debited to Repairs Account.
• Sales Return Book overcast by ₹45,000.
• Credit purchase from Rahul Traders ₹2,10,000 posted to his account as ₹1,20,000.
• Discount Received ₹18,000 credited to Discount Allowed Account.
The Audit Committee asks whether all these errors have identical effects on the financial statements. Which statement is technically correct?
o: Since the Trial Balance agreed, no rectification entry is necessary.
Different errors have different accounting consequences---some affect profit, some affect asset valuation, while others affect only ledger balances.
Every error merely affects classification and therefore does not influence reported profit.
Every error should be rectified through the Suspense Account.
w: Different types of errors have different accounting consequences: some (like errors of omission or errors of principle affecting revenue items) impact reported profit, others (like wrongly capitalising or expensing an item) affect asset valuation, and still others (like errors of posting within the same class of accounts) affect only ledger balances without touching profit — so a uniform assumption about impact would be incorrect.
